summary.short: The bill would criminalize knowingly publishing materially deceptive media within 90 days of an election to deceive electors, and require disclosure of AI-generated content in campaign advertisements. It would take effect on gubernatorial approval or becoming law.
summary.long: SB 9 would add Code Section 21-2-605 to Georgia's election code, creating the offenses of fraudulent election interference and solicitation of fraudulent election interference. A person commits the first offense by knowingly publishing, broadcasting, streaming or uploading materially deceptive media (video, audio or still images depicting a real individual's speech or conduct that did not occur and would appear authentic to a reasonable observer) within 90 days of an election, with intent to deceive electors. A first offense is a misdemeanor; a second or subsequent offense is a felony punishable by two to five years' imprisonment and a fine not to exceed $50,000. Activity protected by the First Amendment, including satire, parody and bona fide journalism, is excluded. New Article 5 of Chapter 5 allows campaign advertisements to use AI-generated content if they disclose the sponsoring candidate or committee, any impersonated person, that events may not have occurred, and that artificial intelligence was used. Violations carry a fine of at least $10,000, and AI-generated fundraising solicitations also require disgorgement of funds raised. Injunctive relief may be sought by the depicted individual, the Attorney General or an injured candidate. Prosecution requires a recommendation from the State Election Board. The Act takes effect upon approval by the Governor or upon becoming law without such approval.

relations.note: New 21-5-93(a) makes violations punishable by a fine under Code Section 21-5-6, whose text is not reproduced in this bill. New 21-2-605(a)(1) takes the meaning of 'Election' from Code Section 21-5-3.

notes: (1) 'Materially deceptive media' (21-2-605(a)(2)) and 'AI generated media' (21-5-90(1)) are defined separately and differ; the first does not require AI creation. (2) 21-2-605(b)(3) refers to 'such referendum', but subsection (b) addresses elections only, and 'referendum' is not defined. (3) 21-5-91(a) permits AI content in campaign advertisements 'Notwithstanding' 21-2-605, which conflicts on its face with the offence in 21-2-605(b). (4) The amended text of 21-2-31(5) (Sec. 2-2) shows both 'nothing' and 'Nothing', apparently residue of strike-through and insertion markings. (5) 'Commission' (21-5-93, 21-5-94) and Code Sections 21-5-3 and 21-5-6 are not defined or reproduced in the bill. (6) Effective on approval by the Governor or on becoming law without approval (Sec. 3-1). Registry status is pending.
